newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bankers get warning on modernization.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bankers get warning on modernization.

text.p: U.S. bankers received a warning Wednesday from a top Treasury official that if they drag their heels on industry modernization they could be big losers as other players find ways to go after their business.

"Your competitors are going to be way out ahead of you" if the banking industry becomes complacent and does not push for reform of U.S. laws that divide financial services into various comparments, said John Hawke Jr., Under Secretary for Domestic Finance of the Treasury Department.

Speaking to an annual symposium sponsored by the Bank and Financial Analysts Association, Hawke noted that under present regulation anyone can own a thrift institution. In the absence of reform, he said, commercial and industrial firms that wanted to get into the deposit-taking business could simply apply for their own thrift charters or acquire a thrift.
Hawke said while new players could emerge in the absence of reform, banks would be stuck with the limited avenues they now have in insurance and securities.
Hawke said with several inititatives under way in the Congress to overhaul the U.S. financial services "the odds have never been better" that some change will be made.
An objective in overhauling the system is to "bring to consumers the benefits of increased competition in the financial services," he added.

Hawke said that in the debate over the proper regulatory framework for a modernized industry, some argue that banks enjoy a significant "safety net" subsidy through their relationship with the Federal Reserve. But he said the safety net also involves obligations that the banks have and "whether on balance it really exists is a question."
